body_markdown:
More consumers now use AI to manage their money than most credit union leaders probably assume. In a TD Bank survey of more than 2,500 consumers, 55% said they used[AI to help with financial decisions](https://www.bankingdive.com/news/td-bank-customers-embrace-ai-human-customer-service/816203/) in 2026, up from 10% the year before — a 450% increase.


A new generation of personal AI assistants, including Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s dots, and Grok Bot, is bringing this shift into everyday life. These assistants can work across apps and websites, helping people book travel, make reservations, and manage their schedules. As people grow comfortable handing off those tasks, they will expect similar help with their banking. Credit unions should prepare for a member who asks, “I already have an assistant I rely on. How can it work safely with my accounts?”


Recently, JPMorgan Chase said it is[blocking outside AI agents](https://fortune.com/2026/10/15/jamie-dimon-ai-agents-meta-muse-jpmorgan/) from logging in to customer accounts or acting on them, and Citi and Bank of America immediately followed suit. CEO Jamie Dimon told analysts, “You don’t want rogue agents.” A JPMorgan spokesperson said the bank does not allow a third-party agent to reach accounts by obtaining customers’ banking credentials, and it supports customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers.


These lockouts leave a question that the largest banks haven't answered yet: What happens to the people who rely on AI assistants anyway?


Credit unions don't have to follow the big banks. The cooperative mission of credit unions means they are uniquely positioned to decide whether members manage their money with public tools that no one oversees or with help from an institution they already trust.


### **Members will keep using assistants**


A member whose AI assistant can’t reach an account doesn't stop using agents. The likelier result is a workaround, such as pasting balances or screenshots into a public chatbot, where the credit union has no view of what happens to that information. Not only does that limit the institution's engagement,[consumers](https://myemail.constantcontact.com/How-Credit-Unions-Can-Help-Members-Who-Rely-on-AI-Assistants.html?soid=1103508747234&aid=o2ybw3CT-0I#) say it's a suboptimal experience for them. Nearly three in ten Americans who followed a chatbot’s financial advice said it[hurt their finances](https://www.nerdwallet.com/finance/studies/using-ai-for-personal-finances) . But blocking AI assistance may cost the relationship.


Members are not asking to hand over control of their money. In the same TD survey,[fewer than one in five consumers would trust AI to make financial recommendations on its own](https://www.bankingdive.com/news/td-bank-customers-embrace-ai-human-customer-service/816203/) , and TD’s head of analytics, intelligence, and AI said clients want humans in the loop to check the answers. Credit unions can build on that desire for human oversight by helping members use their chosen assistants safely, with clear control over what those assistants can see and do.


### **Trust is a credit union's superpower**


### Credit unions start with an advantage, and member trust is more important than ever when it comes to AI. PYMNTS reports that[85% of consumers see credit unions as good sources of financial advice](https://www.pymnts.com/tracker_posts/critical-moment-the-ai-imperative-for-credit-unions) and 63% of credit union members would attend AI education classes if their credit union offered them, up from 51% in 2023.
‍


Members also expect protection. In Abrigo’s 2026 State of Fraud Survey of 248 credit union members,[66% said they were very or extremely concerned about AI-powered fraud](https://www.abrigo.com/blog/credit-union-members-want-more-than-fraud-protection/) , including deepfake videos, synthetic voices, and AI-generated phishing emails. Among members who had experienced fraud, 44% lost money and 35% lost trust in their financial institution. A majority named faster fraud alerts and automatic transaction blocking among the protections they value most.
‍


### **Credit unions are well positioned to help AI-assisted members**


Educate your membership with short, digestible lessons on what they should and shouldn't share with an assistant, how to check an answer before acting on it, and how to spot AI-enabled scams. These can play on in-branch screens, deliver via online banking, and go out in newsletters.
‍


Fraud monitoring and alerts should cover activity that comes through a member’s assistant, with automatic holds on suspicious transactions. A fraud loss costs the credit union a member’s trust as well as the member’s money. And help members understand what it means to connect safely.
‍


The big banks are right that handing an assistant a member’s password is reckless, but the answer to a risky door is not a wall. Just make sure the credit union, not the assistant, sets the rules. Use the principles of consent, limits, approval, and audit to guide your rule setting.


● **Consent:** The member decides which assistants connect and what each one can see.


● **Limits:** Each agent gets only the permissions it needs, such as read-only balances or payments under a set amount.


● **Approval:** Anything that moves money waits for the member to say yes.


● **Audit:** The credit union logs every action, so it always knows what happened and why.


Credit unions do not have to copy the largest banks when it comes to locking out AI agents. Members will keep using AI assistants, and the institutions they already trust can decide how those assistants connect, what members know about the risks, and who reviews what happens when something goes wrong. Your credit union has the opportunity to use AI guardrails, education, and protection in ways that reinforce your relationship and mission.
